title: Splenomegaly
subject: Medicine
summary: Enlarged spleen reflects underlying disease; in low‑resource settings common causes include infections, hemolysis, portal hypertension and malignancy. Diagnosis relies on focused history, physical exam and targeted investigations, with urgent attention to complications such as rupture or severe cytopenias.

sections.p: Splenomegaly is a spleen size exceeding age‑adjusted normal limits, usually >13 cm in adults or >2 cm below the left costal margin. Diagnosis is clinical, confirmed by imaging when available.
b: Palpable tip >2 cm below costal margin or imaging measurement >13 cm
May be focal (mass) or diffuse enlargement

sections.p: Severity is graded by spleen length on ultrasound or by how far the tip descends on exam; this guides risk of rupture and need for specialist input.
b: Mild: tip 2–5 cm below costal margin or length 13–15 cm
Moderate: 5–10 cm below or 15–20 cm length
Severe: >10 cm below or >20 cm length, high rupture risk

sections.p: In East African and similar low‑resource hospitals the most frequent aetiologies are infections, hemolytic disorders and portal hypertension.
b: Infections: malaria (chronic), schistosomiasis, typhoid, brucellosis, TB, HIV
Hemolysis: sickle cell disease, autoimmune hemolytic anaemia, hereditary spherocytosis
Portal hypertension: cirrhosis (HBV, alcohol), schistosomal peri‑portal fibrosis
Malignancy: lymphoma, chronic myeloid leukaemia, Kaposi sarcoma

sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic or report left upper‑quadrant fullness, early satiety, weight loss, anaemia‑related fatigue, or signs of hypersplenism (pancytopenia).
b: Left‑upper‑quadrant fullness, palpable tip
Early satiety from gastric compression
Anaemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia
Occasional left‑sided pleuritic pain if capsular stretch

t.b: Is the spleen enlarged and are there signs of portal hypertension? – Confirms size, texture, portal vein diameter (>13 mm) and collaterals.
Is there cytopenia suggesting hypersplenism? – Low Hb, platelets, or WBC supports sequestration or marrow disease.
What cell morphology points to hemolysis or malaria? – Schistocytes, sickled cells, malaria parasites.
Is there intravascular hemolysis? – LDH ↑, indirect bilirubin ↑, haptoglobin ↓.
Is the hemolysis immune mediated? – Positive test confirms autoimmune haemolysis.
Are chronic infections contributing? – Positive serology guides antiviral therapy.

sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening and demand urgent referral.
b: Splenic rupture (acute abdomen, shock)
Severe cytopenias causing bleeding or infection
Progressive portal hypertension with variceal bleed
High‑output heart failure from massive sequestration

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first; supportive care addresses hypersplenism and prevents rupture.
b: Infection: antimalarials (artesunate), praziquantel for schistosomiasis, antibiotics for typhoid/brucellosis, anti‑TB regimen, ART for HIV.
Hemolysis: steroids for immune haemolysis, folic acid supplementation, avoid drugs that worsen hemolysis (e.g., sulfa drugs in G6PD deficiency).
Portal hypertension: beta‑blockers (propranolol) to reduce variceal bleed risk, consider endoscopic banding if available.
Severe cytopenia: transfuse packed RBCs or platelets; consider splenectomy only in refractory cases and when surgical safety is assured.

sections.p: Regular monitoring prevents progression and catches complications early.
b: Repeat spleen size and CBC every 3–6 months
Vaccinate against encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, Hib, meningococcus) if functional asplenia develops
Educate on avoiding trauma to the left abdomen
Screen for chronic infections (HBV, HIV) annually

sections.p: Conditions that mimic splenomegaly on exam or imaging.
b: Left‑sided pleural effusion – dullness only in dependent area, no spleen tip on palpation
Renal enlargement – located more posterior, not palpable on the left costal margin
Gastric mass – may cause left‑upper‑quadrant fullness but does not enlarge spleen

sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely normal or abnormal in the setting of splenomegaly.
b: LDH may be normal in chronic extravascular hemolysis despite enlarged spleen
Ultrasound may underestimate size if patient is obese; clinical measurement remains essential

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe left‑upper‑quadrant pain with hypotension (possible rupture)
Rapid drop in haemoglobin or platelets with bleeding
New onset confusion or variceal bleed in a patient with portal hypertension

faq.a: The enlarged spleen sequesters and destroys red cells faster than the marrow can replace them, leading to hypersplenism.

faq.q: Can malaria cause a massive spleen?
faq.a: Yes; chronic Plasmodium infection stimulates splenic hyperplasia and congestion, often producing a palpable spleen >10 cm.
When hypersplenism causes severe cytopenias unresponsive to medical therapy, or when a focal splenic lesion is malignant and surgery is feasible.

exam: A 30‑year‑old with HIV presents with left‑upper‑quadrant fullness and pancytopenia — what is your differential and which test will confirm the primary cause? — List infections, hemolysis and portal hypertension; order CBC, peripheral smear and ultrasound; a positive HIV test plus splenomegaly points to HIV‑related lymphoid hyperplasia.

You palpate a spleen tip 12 cm below the costal margin in a malaria‑endemic area — what immediate management steps do you take? — Assess for rupture, obtain haemoglobin, give antimalarial therapy, arrange ultrasound if possible, and monitor vitals.

A patient with chronic hepatitis B has splenomegaly, thrombocytopenia and variceal bleed — which drug reduces future bleeding risk and why is it preferred? — Propranolol reduces portal pressure; it is cheap, oral, and safe in low‑resource settings.

How does a positive direct Coombs test change your management of splenomegaly? — It confirms autoimmune haemolysis; start steroids and avoid drugs that precipitate hemolysis, rather than focusing on infection control.

What features on ultrasound differentiate portal‑hypertensive splenomegaly from lymphomatous enlargement? — Dilated portal vein (>13 mm) and collaterals suggest portal hypertension; homogeneous splenic texture without focal masses favours this over lymphoma.

A child with sickle cell disease presents with splenomegaly and recurrent infections — what preventive measure is essential? — Vaccination against encapsulated bacteria and prophylactic penicillin until splenic function declines.

When is splenic rupture most likely and what is the emergency action? — Trauma or acute infection can precipitate rupture; immediate fluid resuscitation, blood transfusion, and urgent surgical referral are required.

Why might LDH be normal in a patient with chronic extravascular haemolysis and splenomegaly? — LDH rises mainly with intravascular haemolysis; extravascular destruction in the spleen may not release large LDH amounts.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and systematic abdominal exam reveal clues to aetiology, severity and complications of splenomegaly and guide urgent decisions such as need for imaging or referral.
b: Onset and duration of splenic enlargement (acute < 2 weeks vs chronic).
Recent or recurrent fever, night sweats, weight loss – suggest infection or malignancy.
Travel or residence in malaria‑endemic, schistosomal, or leishmaniasis areas.
Known HIV, hepatitis B/C, alcohol use, sickle‑cell disease, autoimmune disease.
Symptoms of hypersplenism: early satiety, left‑upper‑quadrant fullness, easy bruising, recurrent infections.
Signs of portal hypertension: ascites, caput medusae, variceal bleed history.
Medication or herbal exposure that can cause hemolysis or marrow suppression.

t.b: Look for left‑upper‑quadrant bulge, visible spleen tip, pallor, jaundice, spider naevi; positive findings suggest enlargement, anemia or chronic liver disease but cannot measure size.

Patient seated, arms relaxed; gently push left costal margin medially and feel for spleen tip descending below costal margin. Distance in cm below margin grades severity (2‑5 cm mild, 5‑10 cm moderate, >10 cm severe). Cannot differentiate cause.
Percuss left subcostal area; dullness suggests splenic enlargement or left pleural effusion. Positive result does not distinguish etiology.
Apply gentle pressure over spleen tip; tenderness may indicate infarction, infection or impending rupture. Absence of tenderness does not exclude serious disease.
Check for petechiae, bruises, oral mucosal bleeding, and lymphadenopathy. Positive findings support cytopenias from sequestration but do not identify underlying cause.

t.a: Bedside fluid assessment (shifting dullness, fluid thrill)
t.b: Detect ascites which, when present with splenomegaly, points to portal hypertension. These tests cannot quantify splenic size.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Select investigations that answer a specific clinical question; interpret results with locally applicable cut‑offs and have alternatives when resources are limited.
b: Complete blood count – answers whether hypersplenism is present; leukopenia < 4 × 10⁹/L, thrombocytopenia < 150 × 10⁹/L, anemia Hb < 12 g/dL suggest sequestration.
Peripheral smear – looks for sickle cells, spherocytes, malaria parasites, atypical lymphocytes; presence guides specific aetiology.
Ultrasound abdomen – measures splenic length; <15 cm mild, 15‑20 cm moderate, >20 cm severe. Also assesses portal vein diameter, collaterals, ascites.
Serology for malaria, HIV, hepatitis B/C, schistosomiasis, leishmania – confirms infectious causes; positive result directs therapy.
LDH and haptoglobin – answer if hemolysis is occurring; LDH > 500 U/L and low haptoglobin support intravascular hemolysis.
Direct Coombs test – determines autoimmune hemolysis; positive result adds steroids or rituximab to management.
Serum‑ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) when ascites present – SAAG ≥ 1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension; <1.1 g/dL suggests peritoneal disease.
Bone‑marrow aspirate/biopsy – answers if marrow infiltration (leukemia, lymphoma, myelofibrosis) is present; hypercellular with fibrosis supports myelofibrosis.
CT or MRI (if available) – differentiates focal mass from diffuse enlargement; lymphomatous nodes, splenic infarcts, or abscesses are identified.

t.b: Does the patient have cytopenias from hypersplenism? Low Hb, low platelets, low neutrophils confirm sequestration; if unavailable, rely on clinical bleeding/bruising and smear.

What is the size and is portal hypertension present? Length > 20 cm = severe; portal vein >13 mm or collaterals confirm portal hypertension. If ultrasound not available, use physical measurement of tip descent.
Is there active hemolysis? LDH > 500 U/L suggests hemolysis; normal LDH does not exclude chronic extravascular hemolysis.
Is anemia immune mediated? Positive result adds steroids/rituximab; negative result shifts focus to mechanical or infectious causes.
Is ascites due to portal hypertension? SAAG ≥ 1.1 g/dL = portal hypertension; <1.1 g/dL suggests peritoneal carcinomatosis or infection.
What cellular abnormalities are present? Sickle cells → sickle disease; parasites → malaria; spherocytes → hereditary spherocytosis; atypical lymphocytes → EBV/CMV.
Is there marrow infiltration? Hypercellular with fibrosis = myelofibrosis; clonal B‑cell population = CLL/SMZL. If unavailable, use CBC trends and imaging.

sections.p: Combine clinical size, imaging and functional impact to stage splenomegaly; severity guides monitoring and urgency of referral.
b: Mild splenomegaly: tip 2‑5 cm below costal margin or ultrasound length 13‑15 cm; low rupture risk.
Moderate splenomegaly: tip 5‑10 cm below costal margin or length 15‑20 cm; consider periodic ultrasound.
Severe splenomegaly: tip > 10 cm below costal margin or length > 20 cm; high risk of rupture, hypersplenism, and portal hypertension.
Hypersplenism present if any two cytopenias (Hb < 12 g/dL, platelets < 150 × 10⁹/L, neutrophils < 4 × 10⁹/L).
Portal‑hypertensive splenomegaly diagnosed when splenomegaly coexists with SAAG ≥ 1.1 g/dL, varices or ascites.
Lymphomatous splenomegaly suggested by focal lesions on imaging, B‑symptoms, and peripheral lymphocytosis.
Acute splenic sequestration crisis (sickle cell) defined by rapid spleen enlargement > 2 cm in 24 h with Hb drop ≥ 2 g/dL and platelet fall.

sections.p: Several diseases mimic splenomegaly; key discriminators are history, specific bedside signs and targeted investigations.

t.b: May be mistaken for splenic tip descent. Dullness disappears on deep inspiration and fluid shifts with position; ultrasound confirms fluid, not spleen.
Can produce left‑upper‑quadrant bulge. Liver span > 15 cm on ultrasound, normal spleen size, and elevated transaminases differentiate.
Bulge reducible, cough impulse present. No splenic tip on palpation; ultrasound shows bowel loop, not spleen.
May cause left‑upper‑quadrant mass. CT/MRI shows solid mass separate from spleen; CA 19‑9 may be elevated.
Presents with massive splenomegaly and leukocytosis > 100 × 10⁹/L; peripheral smear shows myelocytes, basophilia; BCR‑ABL PCR confirms.
Travel to endemic area, fever, hyperpigmented patches, pancytopenia; rK39 rapid test or bone‑marrow aspirate with amastigotes confirms.

sections.p: A structured ladder guides acute stabilisation, treatment of the underlying cause, control of hypersplenism and prevention of rupture, with clear points for escalation or referral.
b: 1. Immediate assessment: airway, breathing, circulation; obtain vitals, look for shock or acute abdomen.
2. Stabilise: IV crystalloids, blood products if haemorrhagic shock, give broad‑spectrum antibiotics if infection is possible.
3. Identify aetiology: rapid malaria test, HIV test, hepatitis serology, ultrasound for portal hypertension, CBC with peripheral smear.
4. Targeted therapy: antimalarials for Plasmodium, praziquantel for schistosomiasis, antitubercular drugs for TB, ART for HIV, disease‑specific chemo for lymphoma, hydroxyurea for sickle cell.

5. Control hypersplenism: consider short‑course steroids for autoimmune haemolysis, splenic artery embolisation if high rupture risk, avoid routine splenectomy in low‑resource settings unless life‑threatening.
6. Monitor: daily CBC, vitals, abdominal girth, ultrasound size, signs of rupture; repeat labs every 48‑72 h while unstable.

7. Escalate/Refer: splenic tip >10 cm below costal margin, sudden pain, drop in haemoglobin >2 g/dL, or uncontrolled infection → surgical referral or transfer to centre with imaging and interventional radiology.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Key adverse reactions, drug‑drug interactions and actions to mitigate them for the most common agents used in splenomegaly.
b: Artemisinin‑based combination therapy: watch for QT prolongation; avoid co‑administration with other QT‑prolonging drugs (e.g., fluoroquinolones).
Praziquantel: transient hepatic enzyme rise; monitor LFTs in patients with pre‑existing liver disease, pause if bilirubin doubles.
Corticosteroids: hyperglycaemia, hypertension, infection risk; give prophylactic PCP prophylaxis in HIV and monitor glucose.
Hydroxyurea: myelosuppression; obtain CBC weekly for first month, then monthly; hold if neutrophils <1.0 ×10⁹/L.
Antiretrovirals (efavirenz, dolutegravir): hepatotoxicity; check LFTs at baseline and monthly; avoid in severe hepatic failure.
Chemotherapy for lymphoma (CHOP): neutropenia and mucositis; give G‑CSF prophylaxis when ANC expected <0.5 ×10⁹/L.

sections.p: Recognise life‑threatening sequelae early and act decisively.
b: Splenic rupture: sudden left‑upper‑quadrant pain, hypotension, peritoneal signs. Immediate resuscitation, type‑and‑cross, urgent surgical consult.
Severe hypersplenism: platelets <30 ×10⁹/L or haemoglobin <8 g/dL with active bleeding. Consider splenic artery embolisation or splenectomy if refractory.
Portal‑hypertensive bleed: melena or haematemesis with varices on endoscopy. Give vasoactive agents (octreotide), antibiotics, arrange urgent endoscopic banding.
Infection of infarcted spleen (abscess): fever, left‑flank tenderness, leukocytosis. Start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, obtain CT, refer for drainage.

sections.p: Conditions that modify presentation, investigations or treatment choices.
b: HIV: may cause lymphoid hyperplasia, opportunistic infections, and lower CD4 counts; CD4 <200 cells/µL warrants PCP prophylaxis when steroids are used.
TB: granulomatous splenomegaly can mimic lymphoma; obtain GeneXpert on sputum or tissue, start standard anti‑TB regimen, watch for hepatotoxicity.
Malnutrition: blunted inflammatory response, low albumin exaggerates ascites; give protein‑rich diet, correct electrolytes before invasive procedures.
Pregnancy: avoid ionising imaging; use ultrasound, limit teratogenic drugs (e.g., methotrexate), manage anaemia with iron and transfusion if needed.
Diabetes: steroids worsen glycaemia; monitor glucose closely, adjust insulin.
Alcohol: worsens portal hypertension; counsel abstinence, monitor LFTs, avoid acetaminophen overdose.
Renal failure: dose‑adjust hydroxyurea, avoid nephrotoxic antibiotics, use ultrasound rather than CT contrast.
Age extremes: infants may have splenic sequestration; elderly have higher rupture risk and comorbidities; tailor monitoring frequency.

sections.p: Tailored approach for children, pregnant women, the elderly and people living with HIV, especially where resources are limited.
b: Children: prioritize malaria rapid test, sickle‑cell screening, and ultrasound; treat splenic sequestration with urgent transfusion, avoid splenectomy unless recurrent.
Pregnancy: use bedside ultrasound for size, treat malaria with quinine plus clindamycin, give praziquantel only in second/third trimester if needed, monitor fetal growth.
Elderly: higher prevalence of portal hypertension from schistosomiasis or alcohol; start low‑dose diuretics for ascites, avoid aggressive fluid shifts, consider frailty before surgery.

People with HIV: start ART promptly, screen for opportunistic infections, use cotrimoxazole prophylaxis, adjust chemotherapy doses for CD4 count, monitor for immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome.

Low‑resource settings: rely on clinical exam and bedside ultrasound, use point‑of‑care malaria test, treat presumptively for malaria and schistosomiasis when epidemiology supports, arrange referral only for rupture or uncontrolled bleeding.

facts: Adult spleen length >13 cm on ultrasound defines splenomegaly.
Mild splenomegaly: tip 2–5 cm below costal margin or length 13–15 cm.
Moderate splenomegaly: tip 5–10 cm below or length 15–20 cm.
Severe splenomegaly: tip >10 cm below or length >20 cm, high rupture risk.
Schistosomal peri‑portal fibrosis causes pre‑sinusoidal portal hypertension with normal portal vein diameter.
Acute splenic sequestration in sickle cell: drop in Hb >2 g/dL, splenic volume ↑30 % within 24 h.
LDH may be normal in chronic extravascular haemolysis because haemoglobin is cleared by spleen, not released into plasma.

mnemonics.t: Model for End‑stage Liver Disease; predicts decompensation risk in portal‑hypertensive splenomegaly.
Antibiotics, Blood transfusion, Coombs test; initial steps in suspected autoimmune hemolysis with splenomegaly.

vivas.q: What bedside manoeuvre distinguishes splenic from hepatic enlargement?
vivas.a: Percuss the Traube’s space; dullness that shifts with respiration suggests splenic enlargement, whereas fixed dullness suggests hepatic enlargement.

vivas.q: How do you grade severity on examination?
vivas.a: Measure how far the tip descends below the left costal margin: 2–5 cm (mild), 5–10 cm (moderate), >10 cm (severe).

vivas.q: Why is LDH sometimes normal in chronic splenic haemolysis?
vivas.a: Haemoglobin is removed by splenic macrophages without releasing intracellular LDH into plasma.

vivas.q: What is the most likely cause of splenomegaly in a patient with patent portal vein, varices and peri‑portal fibrosis?
vivas.a: Schistosomal peri‑portal fibrosis causing pre‑sinusoidal portal hypertension.

vivas.q: Explain the emergency management of an acute splenic rupture.
vivas.a: Call surgical team, initiate IV crystalloids, cross‑match blood, give O‑negative if needed, avoid abdominal pressure, prepare for splenectomy or splenorrhaphy.

vivas.q: How does a positive direct Coombs test change management of splenomegaly?
vivas.a: It indicates immune‑mediated hemolysis; treat with steroids, consider rituximab, and avoid splenectomy until hemolysis is controlled.

vivas.q: Differentiate portal‑hypertensive from lymphomatous splenomegaly on ultrasound.
vivas.a: Portal hypertension shows splenic vein dilatation, collateral flow, and homogeneous parenchyma; lymphoma shows focal lesions, heterogeneous echotexture, and possible lymphadenopathy.

vivas.q: What are the key history questions for a patient with splenomegaly in a low‑resource setting?
vivas.a: Ask about fever patterns, travel, malaria exposure, schistosomiasis water contact, HIV status, alcohol use, jaundice, weight loss, early satiety, and bleeding tendencies.

vivas.q: When is splenic sequestration most likely in sickle cell disease and what is the immediate action?
vivas.a: Rapid spleen enlargement with sudden Hb drop; give urgent blood transfusion and monitor for hypovolaemic shock.

vivas.q: What does a serum‑ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) >1.1 g/dL indicate in a patient with splenomegaly?
vivas.a: Portal hypertension as the cause of ascites.

vivas.q: Why should prophylactic penicillin be given after splenectomy?
vivas.a: To prevent overwhelming post‑splenectomy infection by encapsulated organisms.

vivas.q: What is the significance of a platelet count of 80 ×10^9/L in splenomegaly?
vivas.a: Suggests hypersplenism; assess for bleeding risk and consider splenectomy if refractory.

vivas.q: How does HIV infection modify the differential for splenomegaly?
vivas.a: Adds opportunistic infections (TB, cryptococcus), lymphoma, and HIV‑associated splenic hyperplasia to the list.

vivas.q: What bedside test cannot reliably differentiate between splenic infarct and abscess?
A young adult with fatigue, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, negative heterophile test, negative CMV, PCR positive for EBV – what is the diagnosis?
vivas.a: Chronic active EBV infection presenting as infectious mononucleosis‑like syndrome.

vivas.q: In a patient returning from a tropical area with fever, splenomegaly and hyperpigmented skin patches, where does Leishmania reside?
vivas.a: Within macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system, especially splenic sinusoidal macrophages.

vivas.q: A 42‑year‑old with shock, melaena, palmar erythema, spider naevi, splenomegaly and ascites – what is the most dangerous cause of his bleeding?
vivas.a: Rupture of oesophageal varices due to portal hypertension from decompensated cirrhosis.

vivas.q: Rheumatoid arthritis patient with neutropenia and splenomegaly – which syndrome is this?
Indolent B‑cell neoplasm with villous lymphocytes and MYD88 L265P mutation – what is the disease?

mcqs.q: Which of the following is the hallmark ultrasound feature of portal‑hypertensive splenomegaly?
o: Splenic vein diameter >10 mm with collateral flow
mcqs.e: Dilated splenic vein and collaterals are typical of portal hypertension.

mcqs.q: A child with sickle cell disease presents with rapidly enlarging spleen, Hb drop from 9 g/dL to 6 g/dL, and platelets 70 ×10^9/L. Which complication is most imminent?
mcqs.e: Rapid spleen enlargement with acute anaemia defines splenic sequestration, a life‑threatening emergency.

mcqs.q: Which drug is first‑line for treating schistosomal peri‑portal fibrosis‑related splenomegaly?
mcqs.e: Praziquantel is the standard anti‑schistosomal agent.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical cause of splenomegaly in East African low‑resource hospitals?
mcqs.e: CML is uncommon; infections and hemolysis dominate the local epidemiology.

mcqs.q: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis, neutropenia and splenomegaly is most likely suffering from:
mcqs.e: Felty’s syndrome links RA, neutropenia and splenomegaly.

mistakes: Confusing acute splenic sequestration (life‑threatening) with chronic splenic infarction in sickle cell disease.
Assuming a normal portal vein diameter rules out portal hypertension; pre‑sinusoidal causes keep the vein normal.
Ordering a Coombs test after splenectomy; it should be done before to guide therapy.
Treating all splenomegaly with splenectomy without assessing hypersplenism severity or infection risk.
Interpreting a normal LDH as exclusion of haemolysis; chronic extravascular haemolysis may have normal LDH.
Neglecting to consider HIV‑related lymphoma when splenomegaly is massive and systemic B‑symptoms are present.
Using platelet count alone to decide on prophylactic antibiotics; functional asplenia also matters.
Failing to obtain ultrasound in a patient with palpable spleen >10 cm before invasive procedures.
